title: Reading the Psalms at length

objectives.can: Read a longer psalm independently, line by line.

explanation.summary: A longer psalm is read one line at a time, with each line's partner in mind. This lesson reads Psalm 103:1–14, a psalm in which a speaker addresses his own soul and then describes the LORD's care in a series of participles and comparisons. Help is reduced: read first, look up afterwards.

sections.heading: What you will meet in a long psalm
body: Psalm 103 is a hymn of praise that moves from one voice to another: a speaker calls on his own soul to bless the LORD, lists what the LORD has done, describes his character, and in the later verses compares human life with his love. There is little story. The grammar you need most is the grammar of poetry: parallel lines, participles used as titles, and comparisons.

The passage for this lesson is Psalm 103:1–14. The rest of the psalm is 103:15–22: human life is short, like grass, but the LORD's love lasts, and the psalm closes with a call to the angels, the hosts and all his works to bless the LORD. You will read it yourself.

The heading, לְדָוִד, sits in verse 1 and is the first word of the text: 'of David' or 'for David', since the preposition ל can mark both. We do not decide here what the heading says about authorship.

sections.heading: Addressing the soul
body: The psalm opens with an imperative, בָּרֲכִי, and a vocative: בָּרֲכִי נַפְשִׁי אֶת יְהוָה, 'bless, my soul, the LORD'. The ending -ִי of בָּרֲכִי is the feminine singular imperative, because נֶפֶשׁ is a feminine noun and the psalmist is talking to himself. In 103:2 the same line comes back and adds וְאַל תִּשְׁכְּחִי, a prohibition: אַל with a jussive, again in the feminine singular.

That feminine singular address explains a feature of verses 3–5 that looks strange at first. The suffixes there end in -כִי, longer than the usual feminine 'your': עֲוֺנֵכִי, תַּחֲלֻאָיְכִי, חַיָּיְכִי, נְעוּרָיְכִי. They all mean 'your' and refer to the soul. A longer form like this is rare in Hebrew and may be an old or a literary spelling. In 103:5 the word עֶדְיֵךְ is also hard: it has a feminine singular 'your' but its meaning is uncertain.

sections.heading: Participles as titles
body: Verses 3–6 name the LORD by what he does, in participles with the article: הַסֹּלֵחַ, הָרֹפֵא, הַגּוֹאֵל, הַמְעַטְּרֵכִי, הַמַּשְׂבִּיַע. A participle with the article is a noun-like title: 'the one who forgives', 'the one who heals'. Each gets an object or an adverbial phrase, such as לְכָל עֲוֺנֵכִי, 'all your guilt', or מִשַּׁחַת חַיָּיְכִי, 'your life from the pit'.

Verse 6 changes the pattern: עֹשֵׂה צְדָקוֹת יְהוָה has a participle without the article, and the name comes after it. The participle is the predicate, and יְהוָה the subject, so the clause says 'the LORD is one who performs acts of justice'. A participle may serve as a title or as a predicate, and the article tells you which.

sections.heading: Nominal clauses, negation and what is understood
body: Verse 8 is a famous summary of the LORD's character: רַחוּם וְחַנּוּן יְהוָה אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב חֶסֶד. There is no verb. The adjectives and phrases are the predicate and come first; the name is the subject. 'Long of nostrils' (אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם) is an idiom for patient, slow to anger.

In verse 9 the lines are paired by negation: לֹא לָנֶצַח יָרִיב וְלֹא לְעוֹלָם יִטּוֹר. The subject is still the LORD of verse 8, and the object of יִטּוֹר, what he keeps, is not written; the first line's idea of anger is carried over. Poetry often leaves the repeated part out. Verse 10 repeats the pattern with the preposition כ: לֹא כַחֲטָאֵינוּ עָשָׂה לָנוּ, 'not according to our sins did he deal with us'.

sections.heading: Comparisons: as … so
body: Verses 11, 12 and 13 are built the same way. The first half is a comparison: כ with an infinitive or a noun, as in כִגְבֹהַּ שָׁמַיִם עַל הָאָרֶץ, 'as the height of the heavens above the earth'. The second half is the main clause: גָּבַר חַסְדּוֹ עַל יְרֵאָיו, 'his love is strong over those who fear him'. The 'as' stands at the front and the 'so' is not marked.

Verse 13 uses the same verb on both sides: כְּרַחֵם אָב עַל בָּנִים רִחַם יְהוָה עַל יְרֵאָיו, 'as a father has compassion on his sons, the LORD has compassion on those who fear him'. The first form is an infinitive construct, the second a qatal. In verse 12 the two halves are כִּרְחֹק מִזְרָח מִמַּעֲרָב and הִרְחִיק מִמֶּנּוּ אֶת פְּשָׁעֵינוּ.

sections.heading: Tenses in poetry
body: The verbs of the psalm do not follow the narrative pattern. Verse 7 says יוֹדִיעַ דְּרָכָיו לְמֹשֶׁה with a yiqtol, a Hiphil of יָדַע, 'cause to know', and the sense is past: he made his ways known to Moses. Verse 9 has yiqtol for what the LORD does not do as a rule, and verse 10 has qatal for what he did not do. Poetry mixes the forms, and the choice between them often depends on the rhythm and the parallel line more than on the time. Read each verb from the context.

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read each verse as two or three short lines. Say what the first line says, then look for how the second repeats, completes or answers it. In verses 3–5, find the article on the participle. In verses 11–13, find the half that begins with כ. Look up words only after trying.

misunderstandings: Reading the -כִי suffixes in verses 3–5 as a different person. They are an uncommon, longer form of 'your' addressed to the soul.
Reading each verb in poetry as a past or present because of its form alone. The form is a guide, but the context and the parallel line decide.
Expecting a verb in every line. Verse 8 is a nominal clause, and verse 6 has a participle as its predicate.
Taking אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם literally. It is an idiom for slowness to anger.

deeper.heading: Why the soul is addressed
body: Addressing the soul is a way of speaking to oneself. The Hebrew נֶפֶשׁ can mean the person, the self or the life, and different translators render it differently. Here it is a grammatical feminine, and the verbs and suffixes follow the grammar.

examples.analysis: The imperative בָּרֲכִי with the vocative נַפְשִׁי repeats the first verse. Then וְאַל תִּשְׁכְּחִי: אַל with a jussive, a prohibition addressed to the soul in the feminine singular. The object is כָּל גְּמוּלָיו, 'all his dealings'.

examples.analysis: Two participles with the article, הַסֹּלֵחַ and הָרֹפֵא, are titles of the LORD, and each has a phrase with לְכָל. The suffixes -ֵכִי and -ָיְכִי are the long feminine 'your' addressed to the soul.

examples.analysis: A nominal clause. The adjectives רַחוּם and חַנּוּן come first as predicates, and the subject is יְהוָה. Then the construct chains אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם and רַב חֶסֶד are further predicates.

check.prompt: Which part of this verse is the comparison, and which is the main clause?

quoted.title: Psalms

options: The whole verse is a comparison with no main clause
The comparison is גָּבַר חַסְדּוֹ; the main clause is כִגְבֹהַּ שָׁמַיִם
The comparison is כִגְבֹהַּ שָׁמַיִם עַל הָאָרֶץ; the main clause is גָּבַר חַסְדּוֹ
check.explain: The prefix כ opens the comparison: as the heavens are high above the earth. The main clause is introduced by the verb גָּבַר, 'is strong', with the subject חַסְדּוֹ.

check.prompt: What is compared with what in כְּרַחֵם אָב עַל בָּנִים רִחַם יְהוָה עַל יְרֵאָיו?

The fear of the sons with the fear of the LORD
A father's anger with the LORD's love
check.explain: The first half begins with the כ and the infinitive כְּרַחֵם; the second half has the same root as a qatal, רִחַם, and a different subject, יְהוָה. The two halves share the preposition עַל.

check.prompt: What kind of clause is כִּי עָפָר אֲנָחְנוּ?

options: A clause with no verb after כִּי: 'that we are dust', with the predicate first

check.explain: After the participle זָכוּר the particle כִּי introduces what is remembered. The clause is nominal: the predicate עָפָר comes before the subject אֲנָחְנוּ, 'we'.

reading.why: Fourteen verses of a hymn in which the speaker addresses his soul, the LORD is named by participles, his character is set out in a nominal clause, and his love is measured in as … so comparisons. All the main habits of Hebrew poetic grammar appear in one psalm.
